extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and aspiring writers interested in Joseph Heller's life and writing process
extracted.subtask_short: writing process advice from Joseph Heller
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia biography of Joseph Heller that includes biographical material plus practical notes on his creative-writing process and the characteristics/themes of his fiction useful for novelists and creative-writing students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Envision first and last lines before beginning
rubrics_metrics.description: Heller did not begin work on a story until he had envisioned both a first and last line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first sentence usually appeared to him 'independent of any conscious preparation.' The finished version might not begin or end with those original sentences, but he usually tried to include the original opening sentence somewhere in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with a striking opening sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Heller often began from a single striking line (example: 'It was love at first sight. The first time he saw the chaplain, [Yossarian] fell madly in love with him.') which led him to invent characters, plot, and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes the opening sentence did not immediately produce a second sentence; at other times it allowed him to write several pages before stopping. The opening can serve as the seed for character and tonal invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid initial mapping of plot and characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually, within an hour or so of receiving his inspiration, Heller would have mapped out a basic plot and characters for the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This quick mapping preceded his actual writing: once ready, he focused on small units (paragraphs) and built outward from the plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work paragraph-by-paragraph and revise thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: When ready to begin writing, Heller focused on one paragraph at a time until he had three or four handwritten pages, which he then spent several hours reworking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes incremental composition combined with intensive revision of small sections before proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold larger thematic shape until about one-third done
rubrics_metrics.description: Only when he was almost one-third finished with the novel would he gain a clear vision of what it should be about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At that point, with the idea solidified, he would rewrite all that he had finished and then continue to the end of the story — i.e., be willing to rework early material once the theme clarifies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to expand a story's scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Heller originally intended his early piece to be no longer than a novelette but was able to add enough substance so that it became his first novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a smaller form if useful but remain open to expanding the work if the material supports it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid constructing books solely to 'say' a philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Heller maintained that he did not 'have a philosophy of life, or a need to organize its progression. My books are not constructed to "say anything."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggests a compositional stance of discovering meaning through character and story rather than starting from didactic intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire and black comedy as central genre characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Heller's work is described as satire and black comedy; Catch-22 is 'a satire on war and bureaucracy' whose title became synonymous with an absurd or contradictory choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: His novels often center on the lives of middle-class characters and use absurdity and contradictions to critique institutions (e.g., military bureaucracy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-centered exploration of sane vs. insane society
rubrics_metrics.description: Catch-22 focuses on Captain John Yossarian devising strategies to avoid combat missions while 'the military bureaucracy is always able to find a way to make him stay.' Heller observed: 'Everyone in my book accuses everyone else of being crazy...and the question is: What does a sane man do in an insane society?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use characters' responses to institutional pressure and absurd rules to dramatize thematic tension between individual sanity and societal insanity.
